title: Just the Perfect Blendship

jokes.text: Larry's delayed, bewildered reaction: 'Lesbian?' — he had no idea the women in Bound were lesbians
jokes.setup: Gina Gershon casually mentions that she and her co-star played lesbians in Bound, assuming Larry knows the film's premise
jokes.punchline: Larry's stunned, single-word reaction 'Lesbian?' reveals he watched the film's lesbian scenes without ever processing what he was watching
jokes.explanation: One word does all the work. The joke is entirely Larry's obliviousness — he watched the lesbian scenes and just... didn't connect the dots. The delayed beat before the word lands sells it. Extremely character-specific: this exact flavor of self-absorbed, sex-distracted cluelessness is pure Larry Sanders. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.line: Lesbian?

jokes.text: 'It's 2... it's 2 girls. I didn't know they were lesbians. Is there some message there I didn't pick up?'
jokes.setup: Gina confirms yes, they were playing lesbians; Larry is genuinely confused
jokes.punchline: Larry's logic that two women together might have 'some message' he missed — as if lesbianism requires a symbolic subtext rather than being the literal content
jokes.explanation: Escalation of joke #1. Larry doubling down — not just confused but now searching for deeper meaning — shows his pathological need to seem thoughtful while being profoundly shallow. 'Is there some message there I didn't pick up?' is a great Larry line. Slightly less sharp than the initial beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I didn't know they were lesbians. Is there some message there I didn't pick up?

jokes.text: 'I'll have to watch it again knowing that.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been embarrassed by not knowing Bound featured lesbian content
jokes.punchline: Rather than playing embarrassed, Larry plays it as a genuine revelation that he'll revisit the film — transparently because he wants to re-watch the lesbian scenes with full awareness
jokes.explanation: The third beat of this running gag. Larry's self-delusion — framing his horndog intentions as intellectual re-engagement with cinema — is classic. Doesn't need much setup because we've already been primed. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maybe we should finish these questions here at dinner and just wrap this thing up. Get rid of Hank and the audience and just, uh... discuss the rest of these on our own.

jokes.text: The promo card says 'Jeff Goldblum' — Gina says 'Tell him I said hi.' Producer says 'Great job with the Gina Gershon questions.'
jokes.setup: Behind-the-scenes conversation about the just-completed interview
jokes.punchline: The casual, transactional showbiz mechanics — celebrities as interchangeable commodities, Gina's friendly 'tell him I said hi' implying industry incestuousness
jokes.explanation: Functional industry-satire texture. The bit about the promo card confusion is a small gag. Not a standout moment but adds to the show's realistic behind-the-scenes fabric.

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.line: Jeff goldblum. You were gonna ask me about Jeff. That's the promo card.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, she was funny, and hot. Good.' / 'So was Larry, but you kind of crapped out with the comic, didn't you?'
jokes.setup: They're debriefing last night's show; the Gina segment went well
jokes.punchline: Backhanded segue — acknowledging Larry was 'also funny' then immediately pivoting to 'but you crapped out with the comic,' puncturing any warm feelings
jokes.explanation: The behind-the-scenes critique of the show-within-the-show is a classic Larry Sanders structural joke. The deflation of Larry with 'crapped out with the comic' is dry and true to the show's ethos, but not particularly sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's Larry for 'I hate this guy.'

jokes.text: 'That's Larry for 'I hate this guy.'' — describing Larry's expression during the comic's set
jokes.setup: They're reviewing Larry's reaction to the stand-up comic Dana Gould on last night's show
jokes.punchline: Larry has a specific, apparently recognizable expression that means 'I hate this guy' — suggesting he deploys it so often that staff has learned to read it
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy. The implication that Larry's contempt is so frequent and specific that it's become staff shorthand is a beautiful piece of character-building disguised as a throwaway line. 'It's so hard to tell what Larry likes' / 'Larry likes Gina Gershon' is a nice two-beat finish.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Lou
dialogue.line: I have nothing else to do.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: That's so sad.

jokes.text: 'I'll go with you.' / 'You totally don't have to go with me.' / 'I have nothing else to do.' / 'That's so sad.'
jokes.setup: Hank insists on accompanying someone to a stand-up spot at Largo
jokes.punchline: 'I have nothing else to do' — Hank's cheerful admission of his pathetic social life, punctuated by 'That's so sad' which Hank brushes off completely
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank: cheerfully unaware of his own pathos. The rhythm of the exchange is well-timed. 'That's so sad' landing with no response from Hank is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: we can go to my house and see a little tape I like to call too hot for TV, totally uncensored.

jokes.text: Hank offers to show 'a little tape I like to call too hot for TV, totally uncensored' as the draw to come back to his house
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to incentivize someone to come to his house after the show
jokes.punchline: The tape — whatever it is — is described with maximum sleaze-bro energy, revealing Hank's vision of a fun evening
jokes.explanation: Standard Hank sleaziness. Not particularly inventive but character-consistent. Gets a mild chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Um... have you ever had a 'collinoscopy'?

jokes.text: The prop comic who once cut his finger off will be at the show tonight — 'Does he do that every time?' / 'No.'
jokes.setup: Recalling a previous show where a prop comic accidentally cut his finger off
jokes.punchline: 'Does he do that every time?' — the absurd question of whether severing a finger is part of the act, answered with a flat 'No'
jokes.explanation: The straight-faced 'No' doing the heavy lifting. The gag works because the question treats a gruesome accident as a potential comedy routine, and the answer refuses to engage with the absurdity. Tight economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Not officially.

jokes.text: Hank mispronounces 'colonoscopy' as 'collinoscopy' — twice
jokes.setup: Hank approaches someone to ask about a medical procedure he's about to have
jokes.punchline: He calls it a 'collinoscopy' — a malapropism that reveals both his medical ignorance and his pompous confidence in being wrong
jokes.explanation: Hank mispronouncing a medical term with complete confidence is perfectly in character. The joke is modest but serves as the setup for the whole colonoscopy subplot. The callback when he gets corrected and immediately reverts adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Hank, how do you ask somebody out who's seen the inside of your ass?

jokes.text: 'It's a little camera, and they stick it up your ass, and it looks around' — Hank's clinical description of a colonoscopy
jokes.setup: Hank is explaining what a colonoscopy is to someone who hasn't had one
jokes.punchline: Hank's reductive, crude-but-accurate explanation — 'they stick it up your ass, and it looks around' — delivered with complete medical seriousness
jokes.explanation: Functional setup joke for the colonoscopy thread. The stripped-down clinical language is mildly amusing but unremarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: How could you tell? Weren't you facing the other way?

jokes.text: 'I think I would remember.' / 'I'm going in tomorrow. I just want to know if it hurts.' / 'It does.' / 'So you've had one?' / 'Not officially.'
jokes.setup: Hank asks Artie if he's ever had a colonoscopy
jokes.punchline: 'Not officially' — Artie has clearly had something similar done to him non-medically, delivered completely deadpan
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first genuine standout. 'Not officially' is a masterclass in economy — two words that imply an entire unexplained history of non-medical anal exploration, delivered by Artie with zero affect. It's Rip Torn at his best. The structure is perfect: question → honest answer → follow-up → devastating two-word punchline. Entirely specific to Artie's world-weary, seen-everything character. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: You know, it usually takes several years to get to that level of intimacy.

jokes.text: After Larry genuinely considers Wendy for the show, he freezes — long pause as he 'pictures her on the show'
jokes.setup: Larry tells Wendy she's better than half the comics they book; Wendy asks 'You think I'm ready?' and clarifies she means for 'our show'
jokes.punchline: Larry goes silent, genuinely calculating the political and professional implications — the silence itself reveals his paranoid risk-assessment process happening in real time
jokes.explanation: A very Larry Sanders joke: the humor is entirely in what he doesn't say. The audience understands that Larry is running through 'what does booking my own writer do to me politically / career-wise' and the comedy is in the visible machination. The 'Why do you do this?' follow-up confirms we read the beat correctly.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I bonded with a man completely non-sexually the other day.

jokes.text: 'I mean, now I feel like an asshole. Do you not think I'm ready and you were just trying to be nice?' / 'No. Yes, I'm... I don't know if Larry would think you were funny.'
jokes.setup: Wendy, encouraged by Larry's apparent enthusiasm, is now embarrassed by his hesitation
jokes.punchline: Mary Lou's 'No. Yes, I'm... I don't know if Larry would think you were funny' — a magnificently fumbled non-answer that manages to be both reassuring and devastating simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The cringe here is earned — we understand Mary Lou's impossible position (she's in the middle of a friendship dynamic), and her answer accidentally confirms Wendy's worst fear while trying to deny it. Good Larry Sanders texture.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: okay. No good?

dialogue.speaker: Mary Lou
dialogue.line: No, I think it might make Larry uncomfortable.

jokes.text: 'How do you ask somebody out who's seen the inside of your ass?'
jokes.setup: Hank describes his gorgeous colonoscopy doctor and muses about asking her out
jokes.punchline: The existential/romantic dilemma: the intimacy of the procedure has outpaced any normal courtship timeline
jokes.explanation: A genuine gem. The question is both absurd and philosophically real — there IS something fundamentally weird about romantic pursuit after that specific intimacy. 'The inside of your ass' is the right level of blunt. Highly quotable, works as a standalone line, specific to Hank's particular situation while being universally relatable as a concept. Near-excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: My neck is 4 inches long... flaccid.

jokes.text: 'How could you tell? Weren't you facing the other way?' — Artie's response to Hank claiming there was 'a vibe' during the procedure
jokes.setup: Hank says he thinks the doctor likes him — he could sense a vibe in the room
jokes.punchline: Artie's literal-minded destruction: during a colonoscopy, you face away from the doctor — so how exactly did Hank receive this vibe?
jokes.explanation: Artie delivers another top-tier line. The structure is impeccable: Hank's romantic delusion is punctured with clinical precision by reminding him of the physical geometry of the procedure. The comedic logic is airtight. Pure Artie — he weaponizes literal-mindedness. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: I think this is a funnier area of the bathroom. I think I could really kill here, yeah. Hey, how ya doin', folks? Great to be here... by the tampon dispenser!

jokes.text: 'Well, granted, I was sedated at the time, but there was a vibe in that room.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just pointed out Hank was facing away; Hank doubles down
jokes.punchline: 'Granted, I was sedated' — Hank conceding the two most damaging facts (wrong orientation, unconscious) while still maintaining his romantic certainty
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Hank's delusion. 'Granted, I was sedated' is doing wonderful work — it's a legal-brief concession that inadvertently makes his case more absurd. Hank's unshakeable confidence in romantic situations he literally could not have perceived is a perfect character note.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: Hey, how ya doin', folks? Great to be here... by the tampon dispenser!

jokes.text: Hank's story about helping a man urinate against his building — cut off by 'No good?'
jokes.setup: Hank segues into a story about a man trying to pee on his building, bonding non-sexually with him
jokes.punchline: The story is cut off before completion by 'No good?' — the suggestion that the joke was flagged as inappropriate or not suitable for the show
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the abrupt truncation — we never find out what happened, and the 'No good?' response to the unseen story creates a mystery that's funnier than any conclusion could be. The setup — 'I bonded with a man completely non-sexually' — is a perfect Hank qualifier. Solid but mid-tier.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Goldblum
dialogue.line: No, these are pajamas.

jokes.text: The story of Hank bonding with a man who was trying to urinate on the side of his building — delivered as an example of important male bonding
jokes.setup: Hank is talking about non-sexual male bonding as something meaningful
jokes.punchline: The context: the man he bonded with was peeing on his building — and Hank went behind him and... [cut off by Artie]
jokes.explanation: The absurdism of 'I bonded with a man who was trying to urinate on my building' as a meaningful connection is very Hank. The cut-off before we find out what Hank did is a smart choice — the implication is funnier than the explanation. The joke is incomplete but the setup has enough.

dialogue.speaker: Phil

jokes.text: 'OK. No good?' / 'No, I think it might make Larry uncomfortable.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just re-enacted/demonstrated something from the urination bonding story
jokes.punchline: Artie's concern isn't about the act itself but about how Larry will receive it — revealing that Larry's comfort is the ultimate arbiter of all behavior in this world
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the implied visual (whatever Hank just did) plus Artie's meta-concern about Larry. Standard show texture, functional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Listen, uh, we were talking earlier in the makeup room. I meant to tell you, you know, I asked out Gina gershon when she did the show.

jokes.text: Artie/Beverly forcing Wendy to audition her material in the bathroom, announced as 'Ladies and gentlemen, Wendy Trastin!'
jokes.setup: The staff needs to figure out if Wendy's material will work for Larry; Beverly is dragooned into being the test audience
jokes.punchline: A full formal introduction — 'Ladies and gentlemen, Wendy Trastin!' — in a bathroom, treating a toilet as a comedy stage
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the gap between the formal announcement and the bathroom setting — industry pretension colliding with tawdry reality. A solid Larry Sanders scene-setting joke that establishes the stakes of Wendy's audition in a characteristically deflating way.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Anyway we're off the air in 2 fucking weeks.

jokes.text: Wendy's neck joke in the bathroom: 'Probably my most attractive feature is my neck. I have a really long neck. My neck is 4 inches long... flaccid.'
jokes.setup: Wendy is performing her stand-up for Beverly in a bathroom — her 'most attractive feature' is her neck
jokes.punchline: '4 inches long... flaccid' — co-opting the language of penis size to describe her neck, creating a surreal and unexpected punchline
jokes.explanation: An excellent joke. The misdirection is clean: 'most attractive feature' primes for a self-deprecating punchline, 'long neck' adds a specific detail, then 'flaccid' lands completely left-field — applying the vocabulary of erectile states to a non-sexual body part. It's absurd, original, and perfectly economical. The pause before 'flaccid' is the invisible punctuation that makes it work. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Beverly's reaction: no laugh, then defending Bill Cosby's dentist routine while Wendy's jokes go unacknowledged
jokes.setup: Wendy delivers her neck/flaccid joke expecting a reaction from Beverly
jokes.punchline: Beverly's deadpan non-reaction, followed by pivoting to explain what SHE finds funny (Bill Cosby), is the cringe — she can't even acknowledge the joke's quality
jokes.explanation: Beverly liking Bill Cosby's dentist routine is a perfectly calibrated character detail — it's the safest, most wholesome comedy imaginable, in direct contrast to Wendy's transgressive material. The cringe of having your work judged by someone who doesn't understand it is very Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: You fucking rule! You fucking rule!

jokes.text: 'I'm in a fucking bathroom, Mary. I'm just doing my job.' / 'Fine. Why don't we start from the top by the fucking tampon dispenser?!'
jokes.setup: Beverly and Wendy are bickering about the informal stand-up audition happening in the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Wendy's furious 'by the fucking tampon dispenser!' — the absurdity of treating a bathroom tampon dispenser as a performance space landmark, delivered with full comedic commitment
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'tampon dispenser' elevates what could be a generic argument. The contrast between the seriousness of Wendy's artistic ambition and the setting (a bathroom, beside a tampon machine) is a good cringe escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Phil

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because I once saw him in a speedo, and I couldn't eat for a week.

jokes.text: Wendy, still furious, breaks into stand-up: 'Hey, how ya doin', folks! Great to be here... by the tampon dispenser!'
jokes.setup: Wendy is angry at Beverly and the situation, but then commits fully to performing anyway
jokes.punchline: She actually uses 'by the tampon dispenser' as a crowd-work opener — turning her frustration into material in real time
jokes.explanation: Nice callback — she takes the grievance and immediately weaponizes it as material. The 'this is funnier area of the bathroom / I think I could really kill here' setup makes it land. Shows Wendy's character: even in conflict, the comedy instinct is always on.

jokes.setup: Larry finds Goldblum in makeup, apparently very physically responsive to the makeup brush
jokes.punchline: Larry's mock-concerned 'I'd be very careful' — treating Goldblum's sensory enthusiasm as something requiring a warning
jokes.explanation: This exists largely to establish Jeff Goldblum as Goldblum — the sensory enthusiasm, the eccentric presence. Larry's reaction is appropriately bemused. Functional character scene.

jokes.setup: Larry has just seen Goldblum play piano spectacularly; he's complimenting him
jokes.punchline: The backhanded compliment: the public only knows you from your association with CGI dinosaurs, not your actual talent
jokes.explanation: Jurassic Park reference as shorthand for Goldblum's popular reputation. The joke is mild — it's a real compliment framed as a slight. The meta-reality of Goldblum playing himself adds a layer.

jokes.text: Larry and Goldblum's elaborate, nervous negotiation about Larry's dinner with Gina — both being performatively gracious while clearly both wanting to pursue her
jokes.setup: Larry reveals he's asked out Gina Gershon; Goldblum immediately goes into hyper-gracious mode, insisting it doesn't bother him
jokes.punchline: The extended mutual performance of 'I wouldn't do anything to undermine our friendship' while both men obviously want to date the same woman
jokes.explanation: The cringe is in the exquisite mutual dishonesty. Goldblum's performative graciousness ('trust your instincts') is perfectly calibrated. The comedy is in how long these two men can sustain the fiction of not caring. Runs a little long but the character work is strong.

jokes.text: 'This is ruining our friendship.' / 'I know.' / 'So let's just pretend like we never thought about me being on the show.' / 'OK, that's a great idea.' / 'Really?' / 'Great.'
jokes.setup: The Wendy/Mary Lou friendship has been strained by the question of whether Wendy is ready for the show
jokes.punchline: The speed with which both agree to 'forget it' — and Mary Lou's flat 'Great' — implies she's been waiting for this exit
jokes.explanation: The cringe resolution. Mary Lou's enthusiastic 'Great!' is a perfect tell — she was clearly more bothered than she let on. The sequence of 'Really?' followed by another flat 'Great' is a nice extra beat that adds a wince.

jokes.text: 'Hey, Phil, do you like women's basketball?' / 'I don't know. What do they wear?'
jokes.setup: Hank has been abandoned by his friends who all beg off the Sparks game; he asks Phil as a last resort
jokes.punchline: Phil's 'What do they wear?' — his only criterion for attending is the attractiveness of the uniform, a perfectly cynical/sleazy non-answer
jokes.explanation: A clean, efficient punchline. The question 'What do they wear?' reframes sports fandom entirely as a function of female attractiveness. Economy is its main virtue.

jokes.text: 'All those years as Liberace's protégé paid off.' — Larry's on-air quip after Jeff Goldblum's piano number
jokes.setup: Jeff Goldblum has just performed an impressive piano number on the show
jokes.punchline: Larry attributes the skill to Goldblum being 'Liberace's protégé' — a gay coding joke about the performance style, very 1990s talk show register
jokes.explanation: A period-specific joke that relies on Liberace's known gay identity as punchline. It's a functional talk-show quip — the kind Larry would actually say — but it's not particularly inventive and hasn't aged especially well. Character-authentic though.

jokes.text: 'Well, I think that's ridiculous. He really has no right to be upset about this.' — Gina, after Larry says Goldblum was 'a little upset'
jokes.setup: Larry has told Gina that Goldblum was upset about their upcoming dinner; both clearly want validation
jokes.punchline: Gina's immediate, emphatic dismissal — 'he has no right to be upset' — reveals her own investment in the situation
jokes.explanation: Situational comedy of the love triangle playing out. More plot than joke, but the energy of Gina's dismissal reveals she's not as breezy as she performs.

jokes.text: 'Why don't we all just get together?' — Larry's solution to the Goldblum/Gina awkwardness
jokes.setup: Larry and Gina are both saying they don't want to cause discomfort in Goldblum; the tension is mounting
jokes.punchline: Larry's cheerful 'Why don't we all just get together?' — an objectively insane suggestion that pretends solving the love triangle is as simple as a group dinner
jokes.explanation: Larry's conflict-avoidance manifested as a completely unworkable plan. Very Larry: he processes every problem as something that can be resolved with a social event. The comedy is in the gap between the suggestion's cheeriness and its absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy

jokes.text: 'As long as I've been living, the French have been fucking us.' — Artie's observation about Montreal comedy festival
jokes.setup: Artie and others are listing comics who are all unavailable because they're at the Montreal comedy festival
jokes.punchline: Artie's sudden Francophobic editorializing — pivoting a scheduling problem into a geopolitical grievance with perfect deadpan
jokes.explanation: A beautiful Artie non-sequitur. The pivot from 'where are all our comics' to 'the French have been fucking us' is swift, unexpected, and completely in character — Artie as a man who carries decades of industry grudges and generalizes them freely. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: And all of a sudden, I'm thinking, 'oh, my God. I'm turning into my mother.'

jokes.text: Artie: 'Alan King. Oh! He'd be great, but I had a thing with one of his exes.'
jokes.setup: Staff is running through comics who aren't at Montreal; Alan King is suggested
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately endorses him — then disqualifies him because of a past romantic entanglement with one of his exes — treating personal history as a legitimate booking obstacle
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie life-detail dropped in as a total aside. The implication that Artie has romantic complications with Alan King's exes is both absurd and completely believable for this character. Good economy — one clause does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: Especially because he didn't do anything.

jokes.text: The reveal that Artie is booking Wendy in part because 'we're off the air in 2 fucking weeks'
jokes.setup: After elaborate deliberation about whether Wendy is ready, Artie gives the real reason for booking her
jokes.punchline: 'Anyway, we're off the air in 2 fucking weeks' — the show's impending cancellation dissolves all the stakes the scene has built
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent joke and one of the episode's best moments. The structure is perfect: the whole scene has been building real stakes (Is she ready? Will Larry like her? Is Mary Lou undermining her?) and then Artie punctures it all with the show's cancellation — recontextualizing every previous concern as meaningless. Dark, specific, and character-defining. Artie's 'what the hell, she's family' followed by the cancellation reveal is a masterful tonal shift.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: In this business, shows come and go. And friendships, well... they come and go, too, but as long as you kill, everybody's happy.

jokes.text: Wendy's explosion of joy: 'You fucking rule! You fucking rule!' followed by Artie's 'Don't overreact.' / 'That's better.'
jokes.setup: Wendy has just been told she's going to be on the show; she erupts with profane gratitude
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Don't overreact' — and then, when she dials back, his approving 'That's better' — a perfectly paternal deflation
jokes.explanation: Artie's management of Wendy's enthusiasm is warm and dry simultaneously. 'That's better' after she calms down is a perfect beat — it treats her emotional explosion as a volume problem to be corrected, not celebrated. Beautiful Artie character work.

dialogue.speaker: Phil

jokes.text: 'This is called a cyc.' / 'A cyc.' — Larry explaining technical theater terminology in a completely reverent tone
jokes.setup: Larry continues the tour, naming things
jokes.punchline: The guest repeating 'A cyc' with identical gravity — the mutual seriousness about a mundane backdrop
jokes.explanation: The tiniest gag — the solemnity of naming a theatrical cyclorama as if it's significant. Works as texture, not as a standalone joke. Below average.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I can't wait for Larry to meet you.' / 'He's gonna love you.' / 'You know, I've actually been to the show before.' / 'You've been backstage.' / 'You know what I mean.'
jokes.setup: Larry is enthusiastically escorting Dr. Gordon, treating this as a special tour
jokes.punchline: She has to gently inform him she's been to the show; he immediately pivots to 'but not backstage' to save face
jokes.explanation: Larry's ego needing the backstage tour to be special, even when corrected. The 'you know what I mean' is a gracious save. Good Larry texture.

jokes.text: Phil's question about dating Hank after seeing 'inside': 'Because I once saw him in a speedo, and I couldn't eat for a week.'
jokes.setup: Phil asks Dr. Gordon how she can date Hank after having performed a colonoscopy on him
jokes.punchline: Phil's pivot: not the colonoscopy that would be off-putting, but seeing Hank in a speedo — which was apparently more traumatic
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection. The setup implies the joke is about colonoscopy intimacy, but Phil redirects to Hank's physical appearance in a speedo as the more disturbing image — reframing Hank's body as worse than his anatomy. 'Couldn't eat for a week' is the right level of hyperbole. Highly quotable as a standalone insult structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: As close as I've seen.

jokes.text: Artie cutting off Phil: 'OK. Showtime at the Apollo is over. Let's say good-night to Slappy White.'
jokes.setup: Phil has been entertaining the group at Dr. Gordon's expense
jokes.punchline: Artie's dismissal using an old-school variety show reference — Showtime at the Apollo / Slappy White — to shut Phil down with maximum patronizing cultural distance
jokes.explanation: Artie weaponizing his vintage cultural references as a put-down. Calling Phil 'Slappy White' is perfectly aged and condescending in exactly the right way. Character-specific to Artie's sensibility.

jokes.text: Terry Bradshaw's Super Bowl ring gifting saga: 'Super Bowl 9 I gave to my dad. Super Bowl 10 I gave to my older brother Gary. He lost it.'
jokes.setup: Terry Bradshaw is telling the charming story of distributing his Super Bowl rings to family members
jokes.punchline: 'He lost it.' — delivered with complete equanimity about a Super Bowl ring being irretrievably lost by his brother
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the total non-reaction to a cataclysmic fact — a Super Bowl ring just lost, two words, no apparent emotion. Whether this is real Bradshaw being himself or scripted, it works as deadpan comedy. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: On-air: Larry asks Bradshaw what number he wore — Hank confidently answers wrong. 'Hank, higher.' / Hank: '12.' / Larry: 'Why don't we take a break and watch Hank guess the entire current NFL roster and their numbers and weights.'
jokes.setup: Bradshaw has been lovingly detailing his Super Bowl rings; Larry asks what number Bradshaw wore, presumably to seem engaged
jokes.punchline: Hank guesses wrong (too low) then '12' (still wrong), leading Larry to sarcastically offer to 'watch Hank guess the entire current NFL roster and their numbers and weights' — a perfect talk-show put-down of his co-host on live television
jokes.explanation: This is the on-air Larry Sanders dynamic at its best: Larry publicly humiliating Hank with plausible deniability ('it was a joke'). The escalation to 'weights' is the right absurdist extension. Bradshaw's presence makes this land harder — Hank is failing at basic sports knowledge in front of a four-time Super Bowl champion. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Larry asks Terry Bradshaw: 'What number was Terry?' — referring to Terry Bradshaw himself
jokes.setup: Larry is interviewing Terry Bradshaw about his football career
jokes.punchline: He asks Bradshaw what his own jersey number was — referring to him in the third person by his own first name — suggesting Larry doesn't actually know who he's interviewing
jokes.explanation: This is quietly one of the best jokes in the episode. Larry asks 'what number was Terry?' to Terry Bradshaw's face — the third-person reference to the man sitting across from him suggests he's reading from a prep card and has completely lost track of who the subject is. It's a perfect distillation of Larry's fundamental disconnect from his own show, and Hank's wrong guesses ('3,' '12') add a layer. High character integration — this could only be Larry. The joke is even richer on rewatch when you understand the full Larry-as-oblivious-host pattern.

jokes.text: 'I sent her Bob Costas. I sent her Brent Musburger. John Madden drove all the way across the country just to see her. Howie Long goes once a week.'
jokes.setup: Hank is pointing out his colonoscopy doctor to Terry Bradshaw in the audience, bragging about having referred her business
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of sports broadcaster celebrity referrals — culminating in 'Howie goes once a week' as the absurd peak
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the sports-broadcaster list (not just celebrities — specifically sports broadcasters, which connects to Bradshaw's presence) is very well-chosen. 'Howie goes once a week' implies either tremendous hypochondria or a very different kind of appointment. The escalation works.

jokes.text: 'I mean, she gives great scope, you know?' — Hank's sign-off on the doctor discussion
jokes.setup: Bradshaw says all his broadcaster colleagues are 'satisfied' customers of the colonoscopy doctor
jokes.punchline: 'She gives great scope' — a double entendre (scope the instrument / scope as in 'great' in slang) delivered as a sincere compliment
jokes.explanation: The pun is clean and earns its place. 'Gives great scope' works on both levels simultaneously — medical instrument and general excellence — and Hank's oblivious delivery (does he know it's a pun?) adds a layer. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: 'When you walk out there, don't forget to stand on the star.' / 'You mean Larry?' / 'Oh, ha! You see? You're gonna kill 'em.'
jokes.setup: Artie gives pre-show advice to Wendy — stand on the star (the floor mark for the guest chair position)
jokes.punchline: Wendy mistakes 'the star' for referring to Larry Sanders — and her instinct to joke about it is Artie's confirmation that she's ready
jokes.explanation: A beautifully layered joke. The misdirection (floor marker vs. Larry's ego/celebrity) works as wordplay and as character comedy simultaneously. The punchline works on two levels: Larry-as-star satirizes his ego, AND the fact that Wendy instantly makes this joke proves she belongs. Artie's 'Oh, ha! You see?' as validation is the perfect button. One of the episode's strongest moments.

jokes.text: Wendy's Ron Jeremy masturbating with his pinky out joke: '...he's got his pinky out, and I found out why he does that. It's because he's classy.'
jokes.setup: Wendy sets up a story about watching Ron Jeremy, who masturbates with his pinky out — implying there will be some gross explanation
jokes.punchline: 'Because he's classy.' — the punchline pivots from the expected phallic/technical explanation to a social-grace observation, reframing masturbation as a matter of etiquette
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The structure is immaculate: a transgressive premise (watching porn with Ron Jeremy) that signals one kind of punchline, a highly specific detail (pinky out during masturbation), a false-build ('I found out why'), and then the devastating pivot to 'because he's classy' — applying the language of high-society etiquette to the least classy act imaginable. The misdirection is complete and the punchline is completely unexpected. The audience laugh track (inferred from the live show context) confirms the reaction. Highly quotable, endlessly repeatable. Economy is near-perfect. This is close to the 8.5 anchor quality.

jokes.text: Wendy on stage: 'So I'm sitting at home this morning, watching porn as I'm wont to do from time to time...'
jokes.setup: Wendy opens her set with a casual admission of morning porn-watching, delivered with the breezy normality of saying 'I was reading the paper'
jokes.punchline: 'As I'm wont to do from time to time' — the formal, almost elegant phrasing ('wont to do') applied to pornography consumption
jokes.explanation: A strong opening line for a stand-up set. The joke is in the register clash — 'wont to do' is archaic formal English applied to porn-watching. It establishes Wendy's voice (comfortable, self-deprecating, sexual but dignified) immediately and efficiently. Good construction.

jokes.text: Wendy: 'It's a series of vignettes, this particular porn movie starring Ron Jeremy.' [pause for audience laughter] 'Thank you...'
jokes.setup: Wendy describes the porn she was watching, specifying its artistic structure ('series of vignettes')
jokes.punchline: The 'Thank you' after the audience laughs at Ron Jeremy's name alone — Wendy acknowledging that just naming him gets a reaction, playing the meta-awareness of his cultural notoriety
jokes.explanation: The 'vignettes' framing is the real joke — again the register clash, treating porn as film criticism. 'Thank you' after Ron Jeremy's name is a good meta-beat that acknowledges the audience reaction. Solid stand-up construction.

jokes.text: Wendy's neck/flaccid joke performed on the actual show: 'My neck is 4 inches long flaccid.'
jokes.setup: Wendy repeats the neck joke she rehearsed in the bathroom earlier
jokes.punchline: 'Flaccid' applied to neck length — as before
jokes.explanation: Same joke as #22 but scored as a callback in context. The impact is slightly lower on rewatch because the audience already heard it in the bathroom. However, the live-show context and the established stakes (will Larry laugh?) give it additional weight. The craft scores remain the same as the first delivery.

jokes.text: Wendy's 'doctor spanked me at birth' bit: 'I understand that the doctor had to spank me when I was born... but I don't see why he had to call me a whore.'
jokes.setup: Wendy starts a relatable premise — doctor spanking a newborn is a known medical procedure
jokes.punchline: 'But I don't see why he had to call me a whore.' — completely unexpected escalation from medical procedure to slut-shaming a newborn
jokes.explanation: One of the two best jokes in the episode. The setup is perfectly innocent ('doctor had to spank me') and the pivot is a complete 180 — from medical necessity to an absurd moral judgment being rendered on a newborn. 'I don't see why he had to call me a whore' is dark, precise, and completely unexpected. The joke works because of the gap between the victim's age (zero) and the adult sexual judgment being applied. Near-perfect structure.

jokes.text: Wendy's 'licking jelly off my boyfriend' / turning into her mother bit
jokes.setup: 'I'm licking jelly off of my boyfriend' — a sexually provocative image
jokes.punchline: 'And all of a sudden, I'm thinking, oh my God, I'm turning into my mother.' — the punchline implies the mother also licked jelly off men, reframing a sexual anxiety as a generational one
jokes.explanation: A very well-structured joke. The 'I'm turning into my mother' punchline is a standard setup but the specific context (sexual rather than domestic behavior) makes it fresh. The implication about the mother's habits is the dark engine.

jokes.text: Wendy's suing-for-sexual-harassment bit: 'I'm currently in the process of suing my boss for sexual harassment... it takes a lot of guts... especially because he didn't do anything.'
jokes.setup: Wendy builds up a #MeToo-adjacent premise — she's suing her boss, it takes courage
jokes.punchline: 'Especially because he didn't do anything.' — the complete inversion: she's the aggressor, weaponizing harassment law for personal reasons
jokes.explanation: Excellent subversive joke. The build ('I'm suing my boss,' 'it takes guts') is perfectly calibrated to prime a sympathetic read, then the total reversal destroys it. This is dark comedy done precisely: it's funny because of the gap between the moral posturing ('I'm suing') and the admission ('he didn't do anything'). The meta-layer — Wendy herself is a writer on the Larry Sanders Show, and this is arguably about her real workplace — adds bonus texture for the audience. Economy is stellar.

jokes.text: The post-show revelation: Beverly didn't advocate for Wendy when Artie asked — 'I told him I don't know. I was afraid.'
jokes.setup: Wendy thanks Beverly effusively for 'making this happen'; Beverly did not make it happen
jokes.punchline: Beverly's confession that when asked directly, she said 'I don't know' out of fear — deflating the congratulatory moment and revealing the bureaucratic reality
jokes.explanation: The cringe reversal works beautifully — Wendy's effusive gratitude collapses when Beverly reveals she actually hedged. It's a bittersweet character moment: Beverly's cowardice is understandable, which makes the honesty funnier and sadder.

jokes.text: Artie's speech: 'In this business, shows come and go. And friendships, well... they come and go, too, but as long as you kill, everybody's happy.'
jokes.setup: Artie delivers what sounds like it will be a warm industry mentor speech about the endurance of friendship
jokes.punchline: The pivot — 'friendships come and go, too' — subverts the expected wisdom, before the real punchline: 'as long as you kill, everybody's happy' — Hollywood's actual transactional truth
jokes.explanation: One of Artie's finest moments in the episode. The speech is structured as a genuine mentor moment — the structure primes a warm conclusion — but the middle swerve ('friendships come and go, too') and final landing ('as long as you kill') reveals the show's dark showbiz truth. This is a thesis statement for The Larry Sanders Show itself: talent is the only currency. Character integration is exceptional — only Artie can deliver this with the right mixture of warmth and cynicism.

jokes.text: 'Hey, where's Dr. Bottom? Aren't you two going to paint the town brown?'
jokes.setup: Artie looks for Hank's colonoscopy doctor date
jokes.punchline: 'Paint the town brown' — twisting the standard phrase 'paint the town red' to reference the colon/feces context of their relationship
jokes.explanation: Two puns in one line: 'Dr. Bottom' as a nickname for the colonoscopy doctor, and 'paint the town brown' for 'red.' Artie's wordplay here is at its crispest. The compression of both jokes into one short line is excellent craft. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'I don't mind her looking up my ass, but John Madden. That's where I draw the line.' / 'He probably thought of it as a fucking tailgate party.'
jokes.setup: Hank reveals he's not going out with the doctor — he found out John Madden has also been her patient
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'He probably thought of it as a fucking tailgate party' — connecting Madden's football association to colonoscopy in a perfectly absurd image
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'tailgate party' is a superb callback punchline. The joke connects three things: John Madden's famous association with football/tailgating, the word 'tail' (the butt), and the image of a colonoscopy as a social gathering. It's the perfect capper to the colonoscopy thread. The setup (Hank drawing the line at Madden) is also funny in its own right — the double standard of not minding the doctor seeing your insides but objecting to sharing that experience with Madden specifically.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Oh, heads up. Here comes the ass queen now.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Gordon approaches backstage
jokes.punchline: Artie's title for her — 'ass queen' — is both a clinical description of her specialty and delivered with the pomp usually reserved for royalty
jokes.explanation: Artie's characteristically blunt vocabulary applied to medical hierarchy. 'Ass queen' is funny because of the regal framing for a gastroenterologist — the 'heads up' announcement adds a touch of ceremony. Good economy and strong Artie character voice.

jokes.text: Larry's extended massage of the doctor's foot — during which she has an apparent near-orgasmic reaction — while Larry simultaneously tries to have a serious conversation about Gina Gershon
jokes.setup: Larry is massaging Dr. Gordon's feet in what seems like a friendly gesture; the conversation is about Gina Gershon
jokes.punchline: The doctor's escalating vocal and physical responses ('Yes! Oh God! Yes yes! Oh my God! Oh!') completely undercut the serious conversation happening simultaneously — ending with 'I have to go to the bathroom.'
jokes.explanation: A sustained physical comedy sequence. The comedy is in the gap between the mundane conversation (Larry discussing relationship dynamics) and the increasingly sexual sounds coming from the foot massage. The 'I have to go to the bathroom' button is a perfect deflation. This requires visual performance to fully land — the transcript gives us the dialogue but the physical escalation is the real joke. Still very strong.

jokes.text: Goldblum: 'Every time I took a bite out of the chicken, I thought it was your eyebrow. I couldn't even eat it.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just described losing his eyebrows to a hibachi flare-up at a barbecue
jokes.punchline: Goldblum's chicken/eyebrow confusion — the texture similarity between charred eyebrow and barbecue chicken making the food inedible
jokes.explanation: A nicely dark follow-on to the eyebrow story. Goldblum's contribution is exactly in his register — earnest, slightly off, the kind of associative thought that sounds like it came from a real person rather than a writer. The chicken/eyebrow equation is gross enough to be funny.

jokes.text: Larry's friend tells him: 'She totally wants to be with you.' Larry's immediate pivot: 'But OK, maybe she does. Maybe she does, but — if I went out with her, would that bother you?'
jokes.setup: Larry's friend is pushing Larry toward the doctor, saying she clearly likes him
jokes.punchline: Larry's acceptance of the premise lasts exactly one second before he pivots to worrying whether ANOTHER friend would be bothered — revealing his paralysis in any situation involving others' feelings
jokes.explanation: This is Larry's defining character flaw in action: even when the path is clear, he finds a new obstacle. The humor is in how quickly his confidence collapses into seeking permission. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: 'I'd trust your instincts.' — Artie's advice to Larry about pursuing the doctor, echoing the exact phrase used by Goldblum earlier in the episode
jokes.setup: Larry asks if pursuing the doctor would bother his friend; Artie urges him to go for it
jokes.punchline: 'Trust your instincts' — the same phrase Goldblum used to Larry when Larry was seeking permission to pursue Gina, now recycled by Artie
jokes.explanation: The callback works because it highlights how Larry is trapped in the same loop throughout the episode: seeking permission, getting 'trust your instincts,' and then immediately finding another reason to seek permission. The phrase becomes a running ironic refrain.

jokes.text: Larry and friend suddenly distracted by Illeana Douglas: 'Isn't that Illeana Douglas? She's hot.' / 'Hi, Illeana!'
jokes.setup: A serious conversation about Larry's romantic options mid-party
jokes.punchline: Larry and Artie both immediately abandon the conversation to notice and hail Illeana Douglas — the discussion ends without resolution, because another attractive woman has entered
jokes.explanation: A perfect Larry Sanders scene-ender: the weighty conversation about relationships is dissolved instantly by a new attractive celebrity target. Both Larry and Artie spotting her simultaneously is a nice touch. The episode ends where it began — Larry pursuing and then being distracted.

jokes.text: Illeana Douglas appears; Artie: 'You look fantastic.' Larry: 'You look beautiful.' — then Douglas: 'I used to go out with Jeff [Goldblum]. Yeah, didn't work out. 2 actors.'
jokes.setup: Illeana Douglas arrives; pleasantries are exchanged; she mentions she saw the show with Goldblum
jokes.punchline: She casually drops that she used to date Goldblum — creating a third woman (after Gina Gershon and Dr. Gordon) in an overlapping romantic web centered on the same two men — and Goldblum's 'I don't really know him' (denying knowing Goldblum while having just been navigating romantic politics with him) is the button
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode-closing joke. The running thread about Larry and Goldblum sharing romantic interests is capped by a third woman being introduced — an escalation of the absurdity — and Larry's deadpan 'I don't really know him' about a man he's been agonizing over all episode is a beautiful ironic button. The episode ends on the fundamental Larry Sanders note: relationship chaos as casual social texture.

jokes.text: Illeana Douglas reveals she used to date Jeff Goldblum — 'Yeah, didn't work out, two actors' — adding another ex-girlfriend to the episode's romantic web
jokes.setup: Illeana mentions she saw the show with Jeff Goldblum and thought Larry was funny
jokes.punchline: She casually drops 'I used to go out with Jeff' — adding another connection to the Gina/Goldblum/Larry love quadrangle
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is structural — every woman in Larry's orbit turns out to have slept with Jeff Goldblum. It's a thematic running gag that caps the episode. Larry's 'I don't really know him' after all of this is a quiet button on the absurdity of his situation.

tmdb_overview: Larry hits on a guest. Hank hits on his doctor. Mary Lou considers letting her best friend be on the show.
